_comment: Every paper in the research corpus, with the tags retrieval and verification use. Ingestion refuses a paper that isn't listed here. After editing tags, run scripts/apply_paper_metadata.py (it updates stored excerpts in place, no re-embedding). Paths are relative to the repo root. merged_from: older source ids whose excerpts this entry replaces (duplicate ingests of the same paper).

papers.evidence_note: 42 recreationally active men with 6-11 months of lifting, 12 weeks; 10RM tested
counts total weekly sets per muscle (every set of an exercise in full); young trained men only; groups under 12 sets were left out of the meta-analysis, so it cannot compare 12-20 sets with fewer
28 recreational lifters, detrained (no training in the prior 2 months), 9 weeks
older adults only (mean ages 57-70), 7 of 22 studies in frail or diseased groups; creatine doses are study conditions; second half reviews mechanisms
n=10 men, previously trained but 6+ months detrained
12 of 14 studies in untrained young adults; tempo compared per muscle action (eccentric or concentric), not total rep duration
systematic review without meta-analysis: 6 studies, 115 participants, 5 of 6 studies untrained, mostly indirect muscle measures
systematic review without meta-analysis: 23 studies, 491 participants, 4 of them theses
hypertrophy from 5 studies, mostly indirect measures (circumferences, skinfolds, BodPod); combining free weights and machines is the authors' speculation
16 resistance-trained men (2+ years of lifting), 8 weeks
ISSN position stand (narrative review) funded by a supplement-industry council, most authors have creatine-industry ties; much of it covers clinical uses, not lifting
compares sets per exercise, not weekly sets; only 2 studies tested 4-6 sets, so it draws no conclusion about more than 3 sets; trained meant 6+ months of lifting
compares sets per exercise; 8 studies, 6 in untrained people; 2-3 and 4-6 sets vs 1 were trends (p~0.09), significant only by permutation test; only 2 studies tested 4-6 sets
the ~1.6 g/kg/day protein breakpoint is a regression estimate with a wide CI (1.03-2.20, p=0.079), not a target; an author has dairy-industry funding
8 of 11 studies untrained; muscle size mostly measured in synergists or by indirect methods, so 'no difference' for growth is weak evidence
protein intake bands are subgroups where effects appeared, not targets; ~80% of participants already ate >=1.2 g/kg/day; industry-funded (ILSI Europe)
measures repetitions to failure at each %1RM, not training outcomes
20 recreationally trained men (2+ years of lifting), 12 weeks
relative (effect-size) gains, not absolute - men gain more in absolute terms; mostly short studies in untrained people; no study-quality assessment
superseded: later meta-analyses (Schoenfeld et al. 2019; Pelland et al. 2025) found no meaningful effect of frequency on hypertrophy when weekly volume is equated
1, 3 or 5 sets per exercise per session, 8 weeks, to failure, young trained men; weekly arm sets count compound sets in full (no direct arm work); 3 vs 5 sets not significantly different
mostly untrained or recreationally active participants; hypertrophy measured in the legs only; aerobic intensity not analyzed
Bayesian meta-analysis comparing the rest lengths studies used; it compares them, it does not prescribe one rest length
effects only at high doses (>=15 min a session, >=6 weeks, >=5 sessions a week), mostly calf stretching up to 1-2 h a day; strongest results from the authors' own group
the long-muscle-length partials result (-0.28, CI -0.81 to 0.16) is an exploratory subgroup that crosses zero; includes theses; low study-quality scores
18 collegiate powerlifters, 6 weeks
